title: Strategic DDD & Bounded Contexts
summary: Applying DDD across a whole system — where one model ends and another begins, how models relate across that boundary, and why this is the natural seam for service decomposition.

slides.markdown:
Tactical DDD Patterns solved consistency inside one cluster of objects — one aggregate. Real systems have dozens of these clusters, often built by different teams, and a hard truth surfaces quickly: the same word means different things in different parts of the business.

"Customer" to the sales team has a sales rep and a deal stage. "Customer" to the billing team has a payment method and an invoice history. Trying to force one shared `Customer` class to serve both eventually produces a class with fields half the codebase doesn't understand and constantly breaks the other half.

Strategic DDD's answer is the **bounded context**: accept that there isn't one true model, draw an explicit boundary around each coherent one, and define, deliberately, how contexts that need to talk to each other actually do so.

slides.subTitle: Where a model and its language stay consistent
slides.markdown:
A **bounded context** is the boundary within which a specific domain model — and the ubiquitous language that names it — is guaranteed to mean one consistent thing. Inside the Sales context, `Customer` means one specific shape with one specific set of behaviors. Inside the Billing context, `Customer` is a different shape entirely, and that's not a modeling failure — it's the correct outcome of two different parts of the business genuinely caring about different aspects of "customer."

The boundary is usually organizational as much as technical: it tends to line up with a team, a subdomain of the business, or a bounded set of use cases one group of people owns end to end. Trying to draw bounded contexts purely from a database schema, ignoring who actually owns which concepts, tends to produce boundaries nobody on the business side recognizes.

The concrete symptom that tells you two things should be separate bounded contexts: the same business word is used by two groups of people to mean genuinely different things, and forcing one shared definition satisfies neither.

Take "product" at an e-commerce company. In the Catalog context, a product has a description, images, and category tags — it's about discovery. In the Inventory context, a product has a warehouse location, a quantity on hand, and a reorder threshold — it's about physical stock. In the Pricing context, a product has a base price, active discounts, and a currency — it's about what to charge. All three are legitimately "the product," and all three genuinely need different fields, different invariants, and different rates of change. One shared `Product` class trying to serve all three ends up either bloated with fields most contexts ignore, or under constant contention as three teams fight over what a shared field means.

A **context map** is a diagram of an organization's bounded contexts and, critically, how they relate — which context depends on which, and what kind of relationship that is. It's a strategic-level artifact, usually one page, drawn to have a conversation about integration before any code is written.

Unlike a typical architecture diagram of services and databases, a context map's boxes represent *models*, and its arrows represent *relationships between teams*, not just data flow — which is why it often reveals organizational friction (two teams who don't talk enough) as clearly as it reveals technical coupling.

slides.subTitle: Who adapts to whom
slides.markdown:
When two bounded contexts need to exchange information, one is typically **upstream** (its model and its changes drive the relationship) and the other is **downstream** (it adapts to whatever the upstream context provides). A payments provider's API is upstream of your Billing context: when Stripe changes its webhook payload shape, you adapt — Stripe isn't restructuring its API around your internal model.

This isn't automatically about size or importance — it's about who has to change when the other one changes. Knowing the direction matters because it tells you where to put translation effort: the downstream side is where you protect your own model from the upstream one's shape, vocabulary, and change cadence, which is exactly the anti-corruption layer pattern covered next.

slides.subTitle: Translating a foreign model at the boundary instead of absorbing it
slides.markdown:
An **anti-corruption layer** (ACL) is a translation layer at the boundary between your bounded context and an upstream one, converting the upstream's model and vocabulary into your own before anything crosses into your domain code.

Concretely: if a legacy inventory system represents stock as a raw integer `qty_on_hand_1000s` (in thousands, a historical quirk nobody remembers the reason for), your Fulfillment context's ACL is the one piece of code that knows that quirk exists, converting it into a clean `StockLevel` value object with a sane unit before your domain logic ever sees it. Every other line of your fulfillment code works with `StockLevel` and has never heard of `qty_on_hand_1000s`.

The payoff: when the legacy system is eventually replaced, only the ACL changes. Without it, that upstream quirk — and every future one — leaks into domain logic scattered across the whole context, and untangling it later means finding every place someone silently divided by 1000.

slides.subTitle: A small shared model, and its cost
slides.markdown:
A **shared kernel** is the opposite bet: instead of translating at the boundary, two tightly-coupled contexts explicitly agree to share a small, common piece of model — a shared `Money` value object and currency-handling logic, say, used identically by both Billing and Payments.

The upside is avoiding duplicate logic and duplicate bugs for something genuinely shared and stable. The cost is coordination: because both teams depend on the exact same code, neither can change it unilaterally — a change to the shared kernel needs agreement from both sides, which is real organizational overhead, not just a merge conflict.

This is why a shared kernel is deliberately kept small and used only between contexts that are already closely coordinated (often the same team, or two teams that communicate constantly) — it's not a general-purpose way to avoid writing an anti-corruption layer, and using it between contexts that don't already coordinate well tends to recreate exactly the tight coupling bounded contexts exist to avoid.

| | Conformist | Anti-corruption layer |
|---|---|---|
| **What the downstream context does** | Adopts the upstream's model as-is, no translation | Translates the upstream's model into its own vocabulary at the boundary |
| **Effort required** | Low — no translation code to write or maintain | Higher — an explicit translation layer to build and keep in sync |
| **Insulation from upstream changes** | None — an upstream schema change ripples straight through | High — only the ACL needs updating |
| **Right fit when...** | The upstream model is a reasonable fit and you have little influence to change it (e.g. a third-party API you must accept as-is) | The upstream model doesn't match your domain well, or you expect it to change or be replaced |

"Conformist" isn't a failure mode — it's a legitimate, pragmatic choice when translation effort isn't worth it, typically for a stable upstream you have no leverage over anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: Bounded contexts as a service boundary
slides.markdown:
Bounded contexts are the domain-modeling concept most naturally aligned with microservice boundaries — if a context has its own model, its own language, and typically its own team, it's also a strong candidate for its own deployable, its own database, and its own release cadence.

This is a stronger, more principled reason to draw a service boundary than "this feels like a separate concern" — a bounded context boundary already reflects where the *model itself* changes shape and where two groups of people already think about the domain differently. Decomposing along bounded contexts tends to produce services that map to real organizational lines (matching Conway's Law rather than fighting it), and each service's internal model stays coherent because it was already coherent as a bounded context before the service split happened.

The reverse mistake — splitting services along infrastructure lines ("this needs to scale differently") without checking whether it's also a coherent bounded context — tends to produce services that share a model and therefore need constant synchronized deploys, defeating the point of splitting them at all.

slides.sectionTitle: One God model spanning multiple contexts
slides.markdown:
The strategic-level failure mode that mirrors the anemic domain model at the tactical level: a single shared model — often a shared `Customer` or `Product` class, or worse, a shared database table — used directly by every team, with no bounded-context boundary drawn at all.

This usually starts innocently: one team builds `Customer` first, other teams need customer data, and reusing the existing class is the path of least resistance. Over time, every team adds the fields *they* need to the same class, and it becomes a bottleneck no one can safely change — a field rename for the Billing team's benefit risks breaking the Sales team's code, so nobody renames anything, and the class accretes fields from every context that ever touched it, understood fully by no one.

The fix is recognizing this is a bounded-context problem in disguise: each team's actual usage should be modeled as its own context-specific view (a `BillingCustomerView`, a `SalesCustomerRecord`), synchronized via events or an ACL rather than by all reading and writing the same shared class.

slides.sectionTitle: From strategic design to practical enforcement
slides.markdown:
Bounded contexts, context maps, and the relationship patterns in this topic are design-time decisions — they say where boundaries *should* go and how contexts *should* relate. None of it enforces itself; a context map drawn once in a design meeting and never revisited tends to erode as deadlines push people to take shortcuts across the boundary it describes.

Architectural Boundaries in Practice, the final topic in this group, covers how teams actually keep boundaries like these — layering, dependency inversion, aggregate roots, and bounded contexts alike — enforced over the lifetime of a real, changing codebase, not just correct on the day they were drawn.
